notes.title: Chapter map: Idiomatic & structural

headings.text: 🌳 How do I handle a failure here?

notes.html:
Three clusters of everyday language features: shaping data (52–54), failing well (51, 55–56) and text at the edges (57–57a). Read each arrow as a sentence: exception groups built on the exception model.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order: 51 context managers ─▶ 52 dataclasses ─▶ 53 enum ─▶ 54 pattern matching ─▶ 55 exception model ─▶ 55a custom exceptions ─▶ 56 exception groups ─▶ 57 formatting & I/O ─▶ 57a Unicode

🌳 How do I handle a failure here?

The failure notes are alternatives for one question, so the tree lives here, not in each note. (Which data-class tool? is the tree in the typing chapter map.)

What each leaf is, and the one condition that would change the answer:

  • 🪢 except* (exception groups): if you want the results that succeeded rather than the failures, use gather(return_exceptions=True) instead of a TaskGroup.

  • 🚪 context manager (context managers): if the resource must survive a hard kill (a lock, a lease), cleanup code can't help; add a server-side TTL.

  • 🗂️ translate with from (custom exceptions): if no caller branches on the result, a built-in exception with a clear message is enough.

  • 💥 except the specific type (exception model): if the failure is common rather than rare, check first (.get(), in), since a raised exception costs ~4× a lookup.

  • ⬆️ let it propagate: if this is the top-level boundary of a request or worker, catch Exception once, log the full chain, and return a 500.

  • The one big idea: idiomatic Python moves bookkeeping into declarations: cleanup into with, record methods into @dataclass, shape checks into case, retry policy into exception classes, encoding into one decode at the edge.

  • The two most-confused pairs: __cause__ vs __context__ (55: explicit from vs implicit during handling) · except vs except* (56: one exception, first clause vs a group, every matching clause).

  • Ten minutes before an interview: 51's @contextmanager sequence diagram, 55's hierarchy class diagram, 56's split flowchart, then 52's options class diagram.

  • Cross-chapter: coroutine-style generators (throw() powers @contextmanager) · the eq/hash contract (why dataclasses are unhashable) · tasks & cancellation (TaskGroup produces exception groups).

notes.title: Context Managers
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Data model: with-statement context managers · 📘 contextlib · 📜 PEP 343: the "with" statement · 📖 GfG: Context manager in Python

⚡ TL;DR

with pairs a setup with a teardown that runs on every way out of the block, and tells the teardown why you left. It guarantees __exit__ is called, not that your cleanup runs: in @contextmanager, cleanup belongs in finally.

🧭 Flow: with mgr as x: ─▶ x = mgr.__enter__() (its return, not mgr) ─▶ block runs ─▶ any exit calls mgr.__exit__(type, exc, tb) ─▶ normal exit: three Nones ─▶ exception: truthy return suppresses it, falsy re-raises

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does as bind? The return value of __enter__, not necessarily the manager object.
How does __exit__ suppress an exception? By returning something truthy. None or False lets it propagate.
If __enter__ raises, does __exit__ run? No: the block never started, so release anything half-acquired inside __enter__.
Why must @contextmanager cleanup be in finally? The block's exception is thrown into the generator at yield; plain code after it is skipped.
What's ExitStack for? A set of contexts known only at run time, unwound in LIFO order.
✏️ Draw by hand: @contextmanager on error with ─▶ next(gen) runs to yield ─▶ block raises ─▶ gen.throw(exc) at the yield ─▶ only finally runs.

💡 The idea

Without with, guaranteed release is a try/finally every caller writes, correctly, every time. Nest two resources and the finally blocks tangle; put the acquire inside the try once and a failed acquire releases a lock you never held. A context manager moves the pairing into the resource:

class Resource:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def __enter__(self):
        return f"handle-{self.name}"            # this is what `as` binds
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print("exit", exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else None)
        return exc_type is KeyError             # True → swallow this exception
with Resource(1) as h: print(h)                 # → handle-1 · exit None
with Resource(2): raise ValueError              # → exit ValueError, then it propagates
with Resource(3): raise KeyError                # → exit KeyError, then... nothing

Two surprises: as got a string, not the Resource, and the KeyError simply vanished because __exit__ returned True. The file example hides both, since open() returns itself and never suppresses.

The trade: cleanup is written once, next to the acquire, and runs on every exit path; in exchange the teardown gains the power to see and silently swallow the exception that ended the block.

⚙️ How it works

What with does on every way out:

@contextmanager builds that protocol out of a generator's throw(), which is where cleanup goes missing (markers match Break it):

Rule What actually happens
__enter__ failing The block never runs and __exit__ isn't called, so the acquire must be the last thing in __enter__ that can fail.
Several managers with a, b: nests them and exits in reverse order.
Yield exactly once One enter, one exit: a second yield raises RuntimeError: generator didn't stop.
ExitStack enter_context(cm) and callback(fn) register exits; everything unwinds LIFO (three callbacks closed 2, 1, 0).
Async async with awaits __aenter__ and __aexit__; @asynccontextmanager and AsyncExitStack are the matching tools (async primitives).

💻 Code

A request-scoped resource stack: some resources conditional, all released in reverse order, cleanup run even on cancellation.

from contextlib import AsyncExitStack, asynccontextmanager

@asynccontextmanager
async def db_transaction(pool):
    conn = await pool.acquire()        # BEFORE the try: a failed acquire releases nothing
    tx = conn.transaction()
    await tx.start()
    try:
        yield conn
    except BaseException:              # includes CancelledError: roll back on cancel too
        await tx.rollback()
        raise                          # never swallow: the caller must see the failure
    else:
        await tx.commit()
    finally:
        await pool.release(conn)       # every path: success, error, cancellation

async def handle(request, pool, lock_service, llm_clients):
    async with AsyncExitStack() as stack:          # unwinds everything below, LIFO
        conn = await stack.enter_async_context(db_transaction(pool))
        if request.needs_lock:                     # conditional: known only at run time
            await stack.enter_async_context(lock_service.lock(request.account_id, ttl_s=30))
        client = await stack.enter_async_context(llm_clients.checkout(request.model))
        return await process(conn, client, request)

except BaseException matters because CancelledError isn't an Exception: a client disconnect still rolls back, and the re-raise keeps the error visible. Whatever raises inside process, the client is checked in, the lock released and the transaction settled, in that order.

⚠️ Break it: cleanup after the yield instead of in finally.

from contextlib import contextmanager
pool = {"open": 0}
@contextmanager
def connection():
    pool["open"] += 1
    yield "conn"                 # ① enter stops here
    pool["open"] -= 1            # ③ not in finally: skipped when the block raises
for _ in range(100):
    try:
        with connection():
            raise TimeoutError   # ② thrown back in at the yield
    except TimeoutError:
        pass
print("connections still open:", pool["open"])
# look for: 100: every failed request leaked a connection
# naive model predicts: 0, because "with always cleans up"

On CPython 3.12 it printed connections still open: 100; wrap the yield in try: … finally: and it prints 0. In a service this is a pool that drains a little every time the upstream times out, a leak that appears only under failure.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: with evaluates the manager, calls __enter__ and binds its return value to the as name, then runs the block. However the block ends, it calls __exit__: three Nones on a normal exit, or the exception type, value and traceback, and a truthy return suppresses the exception. @contextmanager builds this from a generator: code before yield is enter, after it is exit, and cleanup must sit in finally.

Q · Mechanism — How does @contextmanager turn a generator into a context manager, and why exactly one yield? A helper object's __enter__ calls next() on a fresh generator, which runs to the yield; the yielded value is the as target. __exit__ resumes it: next() on a normal exit, expecting it to finish, or gen.throw(exc) on an exception, so it reappears at the yield line. Catching without re-raising suppresses it. One enter and one exit means one yield; a second gives RuntimeError: generator didn't stop. And on the error path, plain code after the yield never runs.

Q · Failure — Connections leak under load in one service; in another, errors "disappear" inside a with. What's happening? The leak is cleanup outside finally (see Break it): the pool drains only as fast as requests fail, so tests pass and it surfaces during upstream incidents. In async code, except Exception around the yield misses cancellations, though finally still runs. The disappearing errors are a truthy __exit__: a stray return True, return self or return result swallows everything, as does a generator that catches and doesn't re-raise, or suppress(Exception). Return None unless suppression is the explicit purpose.

Q · Design — A handler acquires a DB connection, a distributed lock and an LLM client, some conditionally, and must release them even when the LLM call hangs and is cancelled. One narrow async manager per resource (acquire before try, release in finally, rollback on BaseException) composed with AsyncExitStack, which handles the conditional lock and unwinds client, then lock, then transaction. The hanging call sits inside asyncio.timeout. It breaks at cleanup's edges: a lock release is itself a network call needing its own timeout, a finally that awaits can be cancelled again, and a hard kill runs no Python, so locks need server-side TTLs. I'd watch pool utilisation against request rate, and lock hold time.

⚖️ Compare

try / finally class with __enter__/__exit__ @contextmanager ExitStack
Cleanup lives at every call site in the resource the generator's finally registered at run time
Sees the exception via except type, value, traceback thrown in at yield via each registered exit
Can suppress by not re-raising truthy return by not re-raising if a registered exit does
Common bug acquire inside the try truthy __exit__ return cleanup not in finally assuming FIFO, not LIFO

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "with guarantees my cleanup runs"
    ✅ It guarantees __exit__ is called.
    ↳ Proof: 100 failed requests leaked 100 connections (see Break it).
  • 🪞 "as binds the context manager object"
    ✅ It binds whatever __enter__ returns: a string in The idea. Files return themselves, which hides it.
  • ❌ "If __enter__ fails, __exit__ cleans up"
    ✅ __exit__ runs only after a successful __enter__.
    ↳ So: release half-acquired state inside __enter__ itself.
  • 🔀 Not the same as __del__
    ↳ Difference: __exit__ runs when control leaves a block, deterministically; __del__ runs when the object is collected, which cycles and PyPy delay (finalization).
  • ⚠️ Don't hold a lock or transaction across unrelated slow work.
    ↳ Why: a lock held during an LLM call serialises everyone waiting on it.
  • ⚠️ Don't assume cleanup runs on a hard kill.
    ↳ Why: OOM or SIGKILL runs no Python; locks and leases need server-side expiry.
  • 🔖 Version: with 2.5 (PEP 343); async with 3.5+; @asynccontextmanager and AsyncExitStack 3.7+; parenthesised multi-line with 3.10+; contextlib.chdir 3.11+.
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.

🕸️ Connections

Path: coroutine-style generators ─▶ context managers ─▶ exception model ─▶ cancellation

  • Builds on coroutine-style generators: gen.throw() is how @contextmanager delivers the block's exception.
  • Builds on the exception model: with is a packaged try/finally with a say over propagation.
  • Used by tasks & cancellation: cleanup in finally is what runs when a task is cancelled.
  • Contrasts with weakref & finalization: lifetime-bound cleanup, a backstop, not a replacement.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Go's defer, C++ destructors (RAII), Java's try-with-resources and C#'s using.

notes.title: dataclasses
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 dataclasses · 📘 dataclasses.field · 📜 PEP 557: data classes · 📖 GfG: Understanding Python dataclasses

⚡ TL;DR

@dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from one list of annotated fields, once, at class definition. It validates nothing, makes instances unhashable unless frozen=True, and per-instance defaults need default_factory.

🧭 Flow: class body runs, defaults evaluated once ─▶ decorator reads __annotations__ in order + field() options ─▶ list/dict/set default? ValueError ─▶ generate method source, exec it, attach ─▶ eq without frozen sets __hash__ = None ─▶ slots=True returns a new class

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a default @dataclass generate? __init__, __repr__, __eq__, and it sets __hash__ = None: unhashable.
How do you make instances hashable? frozen=True: immutability makes a field-based __hash__ safe.
Why field(default_factory=list)? Defaults are evaluated once; a factory runs per instance. A plain [] is rejected.
Does a dataclass validate types? No: annotations are only the field list. __post_init__ for invariants, Pydantic for untrusted input.
What does slots=True do? Builds a new class with __slots__: no __dict__, 27% less memory here, no ad-hoc attributes.
✏️ Draw by hand: what each option adds Default: init · repr · eq · hash = None. frozen: + setattr raises · hash. slots: + slots, no dict.

💡 The idea

A plain data class repeats its field list in __init__, __repr__ and __eq__; add a field, update all three by hand. Forget __eq__ and two identical orders compare unequal, because default == is identity. Declare the fields once instead:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
@dataclass
class Order:
    order_id: int
    amount: float
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)   # fresh list per instance
Order(1, 9.5)                    # → Order(order_id=1, amount=9.5, items=[])
Order(1, 9.5) == Order(1, 9.5)   # → True
{Order(1, 9.5)}                  # → TypeError: unhashable type: 'Order'
Order("x", "y")                  # → Order(order_id='x', amount='y', items=[])  no check

The last two lines are the surprises. Generating __eq__ on a mutable class sets __hash__ = None: that's the eq/hash contract enforced for you, since mutable value-compared objects mustn't be dict keys. And the annotations are never checked at runtime.

The trade: one field list generates the record boilerplate, and in exchange you accept its rules: value equality within one class, unhashable unless frozen, and no validation.

⚙️ How it works

What the options generate (dunder names written as on the class):

Rule What actually happens
It's code generation A class decorator that runs once: it writes method source from the fields and execs it. The methods are ordinary Python, costing what hand-written ones would.
field() tunes one field default_factory runs per instance; repr=False hides secrets from logs; compare=False drops a field from ==; init=False leaves it for __post_init__ to compute.
__post_init__ Called by the generated __init__ after assignment: the place for invariants like lo <= hi, not for type validation.
Equality is per class __eq__ returns NotImplemented for another class, so Plain(1, 2) == Slot(1, 2) is False despite identical fields.
slots and kw_only slots=True builds a slotted replacement class (100k instances: 12.0 MB → 8.8 MB). kw_only=True: K(1) raises TypeError … takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given.

💻 Code

The three shapes you actually use: an immutable value object, a mutable record with a derived field, and configuration.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)             # value object: immutable, hashable, no __dict__
class Money:
    amount_minor: int                           # cents: no float rounding
    currency: str
    def __post_init__(self):
        if len(self.currency) != 3:
            raise ValueError(f"bad currency {self.currency!r}")

@dataclass(slots=True, kw_only=True)            # call sites must name fields
class Invoice:
    invoice_id: str
    lines: list[Money] = field(default_factory=list)
    created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    api_key: str = field(default="", repr=False)          # never in logs
    total_minor: int = field(init=False, default=0)       # derived, not passed in
    def __post_init__(self):
        self.total_minor = sum(m.amount_minor for m in self.lines)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    region: str
    timeout_s: float = 10.0
test = replace(Settings(region="ap-south-1"), timeout_s=1.0)   # frozen: "change" = copy

Each option answers a production question. frozen, slots makes Money a safe dict key, shareable across threads and cheap by the million. kw_only stops Invoice("x", [], now) silently binding the wrong values after a field reorder. default_factory gives each invoice its own list and its own timestamp, which Break it shows is not automatic.

⚠️ Break it: a default evaluated once, at class definition.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
import time
@dataclass
class Event:
    name: str
    at: datetime = datetime.now()                         # evaluated ONCE
@dataclass
class EventFixed:
    name: str
    at: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.now)    # evaluated per instance
a = Event("first");  time.sleep(0.2);  b = Event("second")
c = EventFixed("first");  time.sleep(0.2);  d = EventFixed("second")
print("same timestamp? ", a.at == b.at, "| fixed:", c.at == d.at)
# look for: True for Event: both share the class-definition time
# naive model predicts: False, "each object gets its own now()"

On CPython 3.12 it printed same timestamp? True | fixed: False. It's the default trap again: the decorator rejects list, dict and set defaults, but can't know datetime.now() or uuid4() was meant per instance.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: At class definition @dataclass reads the annotated fields in order and generates ordinary methods: an __init__ with those parameters and defaults, a __repr__, and an __eq__ comparing fields against the same class. Because it adds __eq__ to a mutable object it sets __hash__ to None, so instances are unhashable unless frozen=True. field() tunes each field. It never checks types.

Q · Mechanism — Why is items: list = [] an error but field(default_factory=list) correct? A class-body default is evaluated once when the class statement runs, and the generated __init__ reuses that object for every instance: the function-default rule. For a list, every instance would share one list, so the decorator refuses unhashable defaults with ValueError: mutable default … use default_factory. A factory stores the callable and calls it per instance. The check only recognises unhashable defaults, so datetime.now() slips through (see Break it).

Q · Failure — Millions of small records exhaust memory and equality checks are hot. What changes, and what breaks? slots=True: no per-instance dict, 12.0 MB → 8.8 MB for 100k two-field records, and slightly faster construction (66 vs 70 ns). Keep __eq__ cheap with compare=False on large fields, and use frozen=True rather than a hand-written __hash__. The catch: slots=True returns a new class, so monkey-patched attributes raise AttributeError, code reading __dict__ or vars() breaks, and references to the pre-decoration class object, as in a super() closure, need care.

Q · Design — Request DTOs, internal domain objects and startup config for an LLM service: dataclass, Pydantic or NamedTuple? The line is trust. Request DTOs come from outside, so Pydantic: strict, parsed from bytes, a clear 400. Domain objects (Message, ToolCall) are built by trusted code, so frozen slotted dataclasses: cheap, hashable, no re-validation. Config is validated once at startup, then frozen. It breaks in two directions: a dataclass returned straight from a handler leaks internal fields, and Pydantic everywhere inside pays validation on every construction. I'd watch allocation profiles and response-schema diffs.

⚖️ Compare

@dataclass NamedTuple TypedDict Pydantic BaseModel
Runtime validation ❌ ❌ ❌ a plain dict ✅
Hashable only frozen=True ✅ ❌ only frozen=True
Equality same class + fields equals any tuple: NT(1, 2) == (1, 2) dict equality fields
Construct, 2 fields (3.12) ~70 ns, ~66 slotted ~99 ns a dict literal microseconds
Best for internal records, value objects small positional records typing existing dicts untrusted input

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A dataclass checks its field types"
    ✅ Annotations are only the field list: Order("x", "y") constructs.
    ↳ Fix: invariants in __post_init__; untrusted data through Pydantic.
  • 🪞 "Dataclass instances can be dict keys"
    ✅ A default dataclass sets __hash__ = None.
    ↳ Fix: frozen=True; never a hand-written __hash__ on a mutable one.
  • ❌ "The decorator protects me from shared defaults"
    ✅ It rejects list, dict, set only; datetime.now() and uuid4() are evaluated once (see Break it).
  • 🔀 Not the same as a Pydantic model
    ↳ Difference: a dataclass trusts its caller; a model validates and converts on every construction. One job each, never both.
  • ⚠️ Don't use NamedTuple as a domain object.
    ↳ Why: it equals any tuple with the same values.
  • ⚠️ Don't add slots=True to classes that get attributes patched on.
    ↳ Why: no __dict__, so AttributeError.
  • 🔖 Version: dataclasses 3.7+; slots, kw_only, KW_ONLY 3.10+; weakref_slot 3.11+.
    ↳ Note: measured on CPython 3.12.13; nanosecond figures are indicative only.

🕸️ Connections

Path: default trap ─▶ eq/hash contract ─▶ dataclasses ─▶ pattern matching

  • Builds on the eq/hash contract: why a mutable dataclass is unhashable.
  • Is a class decorator: runs once, at definition, and returns the class (or a new one with slots).
  • Used by pattern matching: the generated __match_args__ enables positional class patterns.
  • Contrasts with Pydantic: the same annotated fields, but validated.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java records, Kotlin data classes and C# records generate the same methods from a field list.

notes.title: enum
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 enum · 📘 Enum HOWTO: aliases, auto(), Flag

⚡ TL;DR

An Enum member is a unique named singleton: compare by identity, look up by value, and typos fail loudly. A plain Enum never equals its value; IntEnum and StrEnum do, which is convenient and less strict.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Enum vs IntEnum/StrEnum equality? Plain members never equal their values; IntEnum/StrEnum members do.
What is an alias? A second name with the same value: the same object, skipped when iterating.
Why dotted names in match? case Color.RED: is a value pattern; a bare name would capture (pattern matching).

💡 The idea

Bare constants accept typos like "actve". An Enum makes each choice a named singleton: Status(3) raises ValueError: 3 is not a valid Status, and members iterate as a group. A plain member is not its value (Status.ACTIVE == 1 is False, and json.dumps rejects it); StrEnum (3.11+) and IntEnum equal their values and serialise directly, at the cost of comparing equal to any matching string or int. Two members with one value make the second an alias of the first. Flag members combine with | and test with in.

💻 Code

from enum import Flag, StrEnum, auto
class Status(StrEnum):
    ACTIVE = auto(); DONE = auto()          # auto() → "active", "done"
class Perm(Flag):
    R = auto(); W = auto(); X = auto()
print(Status("active") is Status.ACTIVE, Status.ACTIVE == "active")   # True True
rw = Perm.R | Perm.W; print(rw, Perm.W in rw, Perm.X in rw)           # Perm.R|W True False
# → as commented, on CPython 3.12

notes.title: Pattern Matching (match / case)
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Language reference: the match statement · 📜 PEP 636: structural pattern matching tutorial · 📖 GfG: Python match-case statement

⚡ TL;DR

match checks a value's shape and binds its parts in one pattern; the first matching case wins. Bare names capture, dotted names compare: keep constants in an Enum.

🧭 Flow: evaluate the subject ─▶ try each case top to bottom ─▶ pattern checks shape (type, length, keys, attributes) ─▶ binds names as it goes ─▶ guard if … true? ─▶ run that case and stop (no fall-through)

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does case NAME: do? Captures: matches anything and binds it. A dotted name (Status.ACTIVE) compares.
Does [a, b] match the string "ab"? No: sequence patterns exclude str, bytes and bytearray.
How do positional class patterns work? Through __match_args__, which dataclasses generate.

💡 The idea

Handling structured data with if means two hand-written steps per branch: check the shape (isinstance, "x" in event, len), then extract by key or index. Forget one check and a malformed event raises KeyError instead of falling through. match fuses them:

def handle(event):
    match event:
        case {"type": "click", "x": x, "y": y}:   # shape check + binding, one step
            return f"click at {x},{y}"
        case ["batch", *items] if items:          # sequence pattern + guard
            return f"batch of {len(items)}"
        case _:
            return "unknown"

A malformed event falls to the next case, and mapping patterns ignore extra keys, so a click with a "ts" still matches. Now the sharp edge: case GREEN: looks like "equals GREEN" but is a capture pattern. With a case after it, CPython refuses to compile: SyntaxError: name capture 'GREEN' makes remaining patterns unreachable. As the only case it compiles and matches everything: one("anything") returned captured:'anything', rebinding GREEN in that scope.

The trade: match fuses "does it have this shape?" with "give me its parts", and in exchange bare names bind instead of compare.

⚙️ How it works

How one case decides, by pattern kind:

Positional class sub-patterns need __match_args__, which dataclasses generate: case P(a, b) works on a dataclass; a plain class raises TypeError: Q() accepts 0 positional sub-patterns (1 given).

💻 Code

Dispatching LLM tool calls: structured, varied input where match reads best.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import StrEnum

class Tool(StrEnum):
    SEARCH = "search"
    FETCH = "fetch_url"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ToolCall:
    name: str
    args: dict

def dispatch(call: ToolCall) -> str:
    match call:
        case ToolCall(name=Tool.SEARCH, args={"query": str(q), **rest}):  # dotted → compared
            return search(q, limit=rest.get("limit", 10))
        case ToolCall(name=Tool.SEARCH):
            raise ValueError("search needs a string 'query'")             # right tool, wrong shape
        case ToolCall(name=Tool.FETCH, args={"url": str(url)}) if url.startswith("https://"):
            return fetch(url)                                             # guard: policy check
        case ToolCall(name=Tool.FETCH):
            raise PermissionError("only https URLs may be fetched")
        case ToolCall(name=name):
            raise ValueError(f"unknown tool {name!r}")

str(q) requires a string and binds it, **rest collects optional arguments, and the guard runs only once the shape is right. The names are Tool.SEARCH, not bare SEARCH, precisely so they're compared rather than captured. For untrusted payloads, validate with Pydantic first and match on the result.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A switch compares one value with constants; match checks a value's shape and destructures it in the same step. Patterns are literals and dotted values, captures, the wildcard _, sequences, mappings, class patterns, | alternatives and as bindings, plus if guards. Cases run top to bottom, first match wins, no fall-through. It shines on parsed JSON, ASTs and events; for a few constants a dict or if is just as clear.

Q · Mechanism — Why doesn't case GREEN: match the value of GREEN? In a pattern, a bare undotted name is always a capture target, like the left side of an unpacking assignment: "whatever this is, call it GREEN". It never reads the variable. With cases after it, compilation fails because they'd be unreachable; as the last case it matches everything and rebinds GREEN. A dotted name (Color.GREEN, config.MODE) is a value pattern, evaluated and compared with ==. The other options are a literal, or a capture plus guard: case c if c == GREEN:.

⚖️ Compare

match / case if / elif ladder dict dispatch
Best for destructuring varied structures a few conditions on values one key → one handler
Shape check + extraction one pattern separate steps n/a
Constants dotted names or literals only any expression keys
Extensible at run time ❌ ❌ ✅ register handlers

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "case SOME_CONSTANT: compares against the constant"
    ✅ A bare name captures; only dotted names and literals compare.
  • ❌ "match is a faster if ladder"
    ✅ Cases are tried in order, like an if chain.
    ↳ So: the win is readable destructuring, not speed.
  • 🔀 Not the same as validation
    ↳ Difference: str(q) checks one type in one place: no error messages, coercion or schemas. Validate at the boundary, then match.
  • ⚠️ Don't read names bound in a case that didn't match.
    ↳ Why: they can be left partially bound.
  • ⚠️ Don't use match where Python < 3.10 must run.
    ↳ Why: it's a SyntaxError there.
  • 🔖 Version: match and dataclass __match_args__ are 3.10+ (PEP 634, 636).
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.

🕸️ Connections

Path: names & binding ─▶ pattern matching ─▶ exception groups

  • Builds on names & binding: capture patterns are ordinary binding targets.
  • Builds on dataclasses: generated __match_args__ enables positional class patterns.
  • Used by enum: dotted members are the safe way to match constants.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Rust match, Scala case classes and ML-family languages destructure the same way; except* splits exceptions by type in the same spirit.

notes.title: The Exception Model
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Tutorial: errors and exceptions · 📘 Built-in exceptions · 📘 The raise statement · 📜 PEP 765: no return in finally · 📖 GfG: Python exception handling

⚡ TL;DR

An exception is an object that travels up the stack until an except claims it, carrying its traceback and its cause. Catch narrowly, chain with raise … from, and never return from finally.

🧭 Flow: raise E ─▶ look for a matching except in this frame (subclasses count, first match wins) ─▶ none: run this frame's finally, unwind to the caller, repeat ─▶ handler raises anew: chained via __context__ or __cause__ ─▶ handled: finally, then continue ─▶ top of stack: the whole chain is printed

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Order of try / except / else / finally? try ─▶ except (on error) or else (on success) ─▶ finally (always, last).
__cause__ vs __context__? raise X from Y sets __cause__; raising inside an except sets __context__ implicitly.
Why not a bare except:? It catches BaseException: Ctrl-C, SystemExit, task cancellation.
What does return in finally do? Discards any in-flight exception and replaces any return value; 3.14 warns (PEP 765).
Cost of EAFP? A try that doesn't raise is free since 3.11; a raised-and-caught exception ~76 ns, for rare failures.
✏️ Draw by hand: the hierarchy BaseException ─▶ {KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, CancelledError, Exception ─▶ {ValueError, LookupError ─▶ KeyError, OSError}}.

💡 The idea

Return codes make failure easy to ignore: parse_port returns None, nobody checks, and the crash appears far away with a TypeError pointing at the wrong line. Raising makes the failure impossible to skip and carries its context. The four try clauses run in a fixed order:

try:        ...   # always
except E:   ...   # only if the try raised E
else:       ...   # only if the try raised nothing
finally:    ...   # always, last: on success, on error, on return
# no error → ['try', 'else', 'finally']   error → ['try', 'except', 'finally']

else keeps only the risky line inside the try, so success-only code can't have its own errors caught by accident. And it's cheap: since 3.11 CPython finds handlers in a per-function exception table, so entering a try costs nothing. On 3.12 a dict hit inside try took 16 ns against 21 ns for if key in d:. Only a raised exception costs, 76 ns against 18 ns for .get(), so EAFP ("try it") suits rare failures and LBYL ("check first") suits common ones.

The trade: failures can't be ignored by accident and arrive with full context, and in exchange there's a second control path that's easy to break by catching too broadly or discarding what was caught.

⚙️ How it works

The hierarchy decides what each handler catches:

The left three are "stop now" signals and deliberately not Exceptions: issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, Exception) is False, so except Exception: never blocks Ctrl-C, exit or cancellation. How a raised exception travels:

Rule What actually happens
Matching except E matches E and its subclasses, tried in order, so specific handlers come before general ones.
Chaining Implicit: __context__ set, printed as "During handling … another exception occurred". from e: __cause__ set and __suppress_context__ = True, printed as "direct cause". from None hides the chain.
finally overrides A return, break or continue inside finally discards the in-flight exception and any pending return value (see Break it).
Tracebacks pin frames exc.__traceback__ references every frame it passed, and their locals (refcounting): storing exceptions keeps that memory alive.

💻 Code

A service boundary: translate low-level errors into domain errors, keep the cause, mark what's retryable, never swallow bugs.

import httpx

class ProviderError(Exception):                     # domain errors (see 55a)
    retryable = False
class ProviderUnavailable(ProviderError):
    retryable = True
class ProviderRejected(ProviderError):
    pass

def call_provider(client: httpx.Client, payload: dict) -> dict:
    try:
        resp = client.post("/v1/complete", json=payload, timeout=10.0)
        resp.raise_for_status()
    except (httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ReadTimeout) as exc:
        raise ProviderUnavailable("provider unreachable") from exc      # keep the cause
    except httpx.HTTPStatusError as exc:
        status = exc.response.status_code
        if status >= 500 or status == 429:
            raise ProviderUnavailable(f"provider {status}") from exc
        err = ProviderRejected(f"provider rejected request ({status})")
        err.add_note(f"body={exc.response.text[:200]!r}")             # extra context, 3.11+
        raise err from exc
    else:
        return resp.json()                                             # success only
    # no bare except, no `except Exception: pass`: a bug here must crash loudly

Each except catches only what it can classify, so a KeyError from a bug propagates instead of masquerading as "provider unavailable". from exc keeps the httpx error as __cause__, so the traceback shows the domain error and the failing network call. retryable lets a retry layer decide without string-matching messages.

⚠️ Break it: finally deciding the outcome.

def save_order(order):
    try:
        if order["qty"] <= 0:
            raise ValueError("qty must be positive")
        return "saved"
    finally:
        return "done"               # overrides BOTH the return and the exception
print(save_order({"qty": 5}))       # expected: saved
print(save_order({"qty": -1}))      # expected: ValueError
# look for: both print "done", and the ValueError never appears
# naive model predicts: "saved", then a ValueError traceback

CPython 3.12 printed done twice, silently. 3.14 prints the same, plus SyntaxWarning: 'return' in a 'finally' block at compile time. In a worker this turns every failure into a reported success that never reaches the logs. Cleanup belongs in finally; decisions never do.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: try runs first. If it raises, the first except whose type matches, subclasses included, runs; otherwise the exception keeps propagating. If it doesn't raise, else runs. finally runs last in every case, even after a return. else keeps only the risky code in the try; finally is for cleanup and must never return. Since 3.11 a try that doesn't raise costs nothing, so EAFP is idiomatic for rare failures.

Q · Mechanism — Implicit vs explicit chaining: what do __context__, __cause__ and raise from do? Raising inside an except stores the handled exception as __context__, and the traceback reads as if the handler had a bug. raise New(...) from original sets __cause__ and __suppress_context__ = True, printed as "the direct cause": the right way to translate a low-level error into a domain one. from None keeps __context__ but hides it, for when the detail is noise, like a KeyError behind a clean UnknownUserError. In service code I default to from exc.

Q · Failure — A worker "succeeds" on inputs that should fail, and errors vanish from the logs. What's happening? First suspect: a return in finally (see Break it), which 3.14 now warns about. Then the usual swallowers: except Exception: pass or one that only logs at debug, a broad handler returning a default, a context manager whose __exit__ returns truthy (context managers), and exceptions raised in background threads or never-awaited tasks, which propagate to no one (tasks). Grep for them, and alert on success rate against input validity.

Q · Design — A service fans out to three LLM providers, a vector store and a cache. Which errors retry, which surface, and how do you avoid masking bugs? Classify at each dependency's wrapper and nowhere else: translate library exceptions with from exc into retryable (timeouts, 429, 5xx), terminal (4xx, validation, auth) and degradable (cache down: carry on). Our own KeyErrors and TypeErrors aren't classified, so they crash and get fixed. At the edge one handler maps terminal to 4xx, exhausted retries to 503 with Retry-After, and anything else to a 500 with a correlation ID, logging the full chain. It breaks when an SDK raises bare Exception for everything. I'd watch error rate by class and provider.

⚖️ Compare

Handler Catches Use it for
except SpecificError: that type and its subclasses the normal case: errors you can handle
except Exception: all application errors top-level boundaries only: log with traceback, then fail or 500
except BaseException: everything, incl. cancel and exit cleanup that must also run on cancellation, then re-raise
bare except: same as BaseException nothing: an anti-pattern
except* E: (3.11+) matching members of an ExceptionGroup concurrent failures (exception groups)

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Exceptions are expensive, so check first"
    ✅ A try that doesn't raise is free since 3.11; only raising costs (~76 ns).
    ↳ So: EAFP for rare failures, LBYL or .get() for common ones.
  • 🪞 "finally is just cleanup; it can't change the outcome"
    ✅ A return there discards the exception and replaces the result (see Break it).
  • ❌ "except Exception: catches everything"
    ✅ Not KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, GeneratorExit or CancelledError, by design; a bare except: does, which is why it's wrong.
  • 🔀 Not the same as an error to log
    ↳ Difference: some exceptions are control flow (StopIteration, an EAFP KeyError); others are bugs that must reach the error tracker with their chain.
  • ⚠️ Don't re-raise a translated error without from.
    ↳ Why: the traceback reads like a bug in the handler, and the real cause is harder to find.
  • ⚠️ Don't keep exceptions in long-lived lists.
    ↳ Why: each traceback pins every frame's locals; store str(exc) and traceback.format_exception(exc) instead.
  • 🔖 Version: zero-cost try and add_note() 3.11+; return in finally warns from 3.14 (PEP 765).
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6.

🕸️ Connections

Path: context managers ─▶ exception model ─▶ custom exceptions ─▶ exception groups

  • Used by context managers: with is a packaged try/finally whose __exit__ sees the exception.
  • Used by custom exceptions: domain hierarchies built on Exception with chained causes.
  • Contrasts with exception groups: one exception travelling up one stack, versus several concurrent failures at once.
  • Used by reliability mechanics: retry only what's classified as retryable.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's checked exceptions force handling at compile time; Go and Rust return errors as values, the approach Python moved away from.

notes.title: Designing Custom Exceptions
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Tutorial: user-defined exceptions · 📘 Logging cookbook: context on log records · 📖 GfG: Define custom exceptions in Python

⚡ TL;DR

A package's exceptions are an API: one base class, a small taxonomy by what the caller should do, SDK errors translated at the boundary. Policy on the class (retryable), facts on the instance (keyword-only), and only the message in args so it pickles.

🧭 Flow: SDK raises openai.RateLimitError ─▶ the one boundary wrapper catches the SDK's base error ─▶ raise translate(exc) from exc ─▶ RateLimited(retry_after=2.0, status=429) with the SDK error as __cause__ ─▶ caller branches on type or exc.retryable ─▶ anything not a RagkitError is a bug and crashes

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What should a package's exceptions derive from? One package base class, itself derived from Exception.
How should the taxonomy be organised? By the caller's decision (retry, fix the request, re-authenticate), not by source.
Why keep args to the message? Unpickling rebuilds with cls(*args); a required extra positional argument breaks it.

💡 The idea

Without a package hierarchy, callers catch whatever the libraries underneath raise: except (openai.RateLimitError, httpx.ReadTimeout, qdrant_client…). Every caller must know every dependency and change when one is swapped, and the except Exception at the bottom can't tell a provider outage from a KeyError in the package's own code. Design it instead:

class RagkitError(Exception): retryable = False      # "it came from us, on purpose"
class TransientError(RagkitError): retryable = True  # retry with backoff
class TerminalError(RagkitError): pass               # fix the request or config

Callers write except ragkit.TransientError, or check exc.retryable, without knowing which SDK is underneath. except RagkitError catches everything raised deliberately and nothing else, so a real bug still escapes as a bug. Two SDKs' rate-limit errors become one RateLimited; one SDK's APIError may split into several classes by status code.

The trade: a translation layer at every dependency boundary, and in return callers get a stable error API they can branch on by type.

⚙️ How it works

The taxonomy, with the policy each class carries and the SDK errors translated into it:

Rule What actually happens
Exception, never BaseException App errors must be catchable by except Exception and must not look like Ctrl-C or cancellation (exception model).
Class = policy, instance = facts retryable is inherited by every subclass, so the retry layer asks one question; status, retry_after, request_id are read without parsing messages.
Pickle-safe constructors BaseException pickles as (cls, self.args) plus __dict__ and rebuilds with cls(*args). Bad("openai", 503) with a formatted message failed: TypeError: Bad.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'status'. That matters whenever an exception crosses a process boundary.

💻 Code

The package's whole error surface, plus the only module that names OpenAI's exceptions:

# ragkit/errors.py
class RagkitError(Exception):
    retryable: bool = False
    def __init__(self, message: str, *, provider: str | None = None,
                 status: int | None = None, request_id: str | None = None):
        super().__init__(message)                # args == (message,) → pickles cleanly
        self.provider, self.status, self.request_id = provider, status, request_id
class TransientError(RagkitError):
    retryable = True
class RateLimited(TransientError):
    def __init__(self, message: str, *, retry_after: float | None = None, **ctx):
        super().__init__(message, **ctx)
        self.retry_after = retry_after
class TerminalError(RagkitError): pass
class AuthError(TerminalError): pass
class InvalidRequest(TerminalError): pass

# ragkit/providers/openai_client.py
import openai
def translate(exc: openai.APIError, provider: str = "openai") -> RagkitError:
    ctx = dict(provider=provider, status=getattr(exc, "status_code", None),
               request_id=getattr(exc, "request_id", None))
    match exc:
        case openai.RateLimitError():
            ra = exc.response.headers.get("retry-after")
            return RateLimited("rate limited", retry_after=float(ra) if ra else None, **ctx)
        case openai.APIConnectionError() | openai.InternalServerError():
            return TransientError(f"{provider} unavailable", **ctx)
        case openai.AuthenticationError() | openai.PermissionDeniedError():
            return AuthError(f"{provider} rejected credentials", **ctx)
        case openai.BadRequestError():
            return InvalidRequest(f"{provider} rejected request", **ctx)
        case _:
            return RagkitError(f"unexpected {provider} error", **ctx)

def complete(client: openai.OpenAI, **kwargs):
    try:
        return client.chat.completions.create(**kwargs)
    except openai.APIError as exc:              # the SDK's base, not Exception: bugs stay bugs
        raise translate(exc) from exc

Against a mocked transport (openai 3.23.0), a 429 with retry-after: 2 became RateLimited with retryable=True, status=429, retry_after=2.0; 503 → TransientError, 401 → AuthError, 400 → InvalidRequest, a refused connection → TransientError with status=None. Each survived a pickle round-trip intact. The match uses class patterns to keep the table readable.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: One base class for the package, derived from Exception, so callers catch "everything we raise on purpose" without catching bugs. Under it, a few classes grouped by what the caller does: transient (retry), terminal (don't), and specific ones callers really branch on, like RateLimited with retry_after. Facts go on keyword-only attributes. Third-party errors are translated at the one place each dependency is called, with raise … from exc.

Q · Mechanism — A custom exception works in-process but raises TypeError when thrown inside a ProcessPoolExecutor worker. Why? The worker pickles the exception to send it back. BaseException.__reduce__ returns the class, self.args and __dict__, and unpickling calls cls(*args) first. If __init__(self, provider, status) passed one formatted string to super().__init__, args holds that one string, and cls("openai returned 503") is missing status. Fix it by convention: only the message to super().__init__, everything else keyword-only with defaults, then __dict__ restores the fields. Put it in the base class and add a pickle round-trip test.

⚖️ Compare

Approach Caller experience Verdict
Raise built-ins (ValueError) can't tell ours from anyone else's fine for plain argument errors only
Let SDK exceptions escape callers depend on our dependencies ❌ leaks implementation
One class per raise site huge surface, nothing to branch on ❌ over-designed
Base + taxonomy by decision, translated except TransientError, exc.retryable ✅
One class with error codes branch on exc.code OK for wire protocols; loses except by type

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Mirror where the error came from: OpenAIError, QdrantError"
    ✅ Callers need to know what to do.
    ↳ Fix: group by decision; keep the source as an attribute and in __cause__.
  • ❌ "Put all the context in the message"
    ✅ Handlers need structured fields (status, retry_after); messages are for humans and change.
  • 🔀 Not the same as HTTP status codes
    ↳ Difference: terminal often maps to 4xx and transient to 503, but the mapping belongs at the web edge; the package shouldn't know it's served over HTTP.
  • ⚠️ Don't catch Exception in the boundary wrapper.
    ↳ Why: catch the SDK's base (openai.APIError) so bugs aren't translated into provider errors.
  • ⚠️ Don't create a class nobody catches separately: an attribute is enough.
  • 🔖 Version: add_note() 3.11+; X | None annotations 3.10+.
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.13 with the openai 3.23.0 SDK.

🕸️ Connections

Path: exception model ─▶ custom exceptions ─▶ reliability mechanics

  • Builds on the exception model: the hierarchy, raise … from, add_note.
  • Used by reliability mechanics: retries branch on retryable and retry_after.
  • Used by structured logging: request-wide context belongs on the log record, not on every exception.
  • Breaks when combined with multiprocessing: exceptions must pickle to cross processes.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's exception chaining (new X(msg, cause)) and Go's errors.Is/errors.As wrapping solve the same translate-and-keep-cause problem.

notes.title: Exception Groups (ExceptionGroup / except*)
notes.html:
📚 References

📜 PEP 654: exception groups and except* · 📘 Built-in exceptions: exception groups · 📘 The except* clause · 📖 GfG: Exception groups in Python

⚡ TL;DR

A group holds several failures at once; except* T splits out the T members, and several clauses can run. The variable is always a group, leftovers re-raise, and TaskGroup raises a group even for one failure.

🧭 Flow: children fail together ─▶ TaskGroup raises ExceptionGroup([...]) ─▶ each except* T takes group.split(T) ─▶ its body sees the matching subgroup ─▶ the rest moves to the next clause ─▶ unmatched leaves re-raise as a smaller group

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Does except ValueError catch a TaskGroup child's ValueError? No: TaskGroup always raises an ExceptionGroup, even for one failure.
What is eg in except* ValueError as eg? Always an ExceptionGroup; iterate eg.exceptions.
Can you return from an except* block? No: SyntaxError, because the other clauses still have to run.

💡 The idea

Before 3.11 an exception was one object, so concurrent code that failed in two places had to drop one: gather raised the first failure and lost the second. PEP 654 adds ExceptionGroup(message, [exc, …]), a tree of exceptions, and except*, which handles the parts of a group by type. The surprise arrives when someone swaps gather for TaskGroup:

async def bad(): raise ValueError("bad")
try:
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tg.create_task(bad())
except ValueError:
    print("caught")          # never runs
except Exception as e:
    print(repr(e))           # → ExceptionGroup('unhandled errors in a TaskGroup', [ValueError('bad')])

One failing child, and the old handler silently stops matching.

The trade: simultaneous failures become a first-class value handled by type, and in exchange there's a second handling syntax whose rules differ from ordinary except.

⚙️ How it works

How one group flows through two except* clauses:

Rule What actually happens
Splitting ExceptionGroup("g", [ValueError(1), KeyError(2)]).split(ValueError) gave (ExceptionGroup('g', [ValueError(1)]), ExceptionGroup('g', [KeyError(2)])): same message and nesting, None for an empty side.
Always a group A lone ungrouped ValueError reaching except* ValueError as eg is wrapped: eg.exceptions == (ValueError('x'),).
Leftovers and new errors A bare raise puts the clause's subgroup back; raising RuntimeError inside except* ValueError produced ExceptionGroup('', [RuntimeError('handled badly'), ExceptionGroup('g', [KeyError(2)])]).
Compiler rules Mixing gives SyntaxError: cannot have both 'except' and 'except*' on the same 'try'; return/break/continue inside are a SyntaxError; except* ExceptionGroup raises TypeError … Use except instead.
Base vs non-base ExceptionGroup holds only Exceptions; BaseExceptionGroup can hold KeyboardInterrupt or CancelledError, so except* Exception never pulls those out.

💻 Code

A RAG context step that fans out to several sources, logs each class of failure, and lets one outer layer decide on a retry:

import asyncio, logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
class TransientError(Exception): pass        # the 55a taxonomy, trimmed
class TerminalError(Exception): pass

async def fetch(source: str, query: str) -> list[str]:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    if source == "web":  raise TransientError("web search timed out")
    if source == "wiki": raise TerminalError("wiki rejected query")
    return [f"{source}: hit for {query!r}"]

async def gather_context(query: str, sources: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch(s, query)) for s in sources]
    except* TransientError as eg:
        log.warning("transient failures: %s", [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions])
        raise                                # just this subgroup → the retry layer
    except* TerminalError as eg:
        for exc in eg.exceptions:            # several clauses run for one group
            log.error("terminal: %s", exc)
        raise
    return [hit for t in tasks for hit in t.result()]

async def main():
    try:
        await gather_context("gil", ["docs", "web", "wiki"])
    except ExceptionGroup as eg:             # plain except: the whole group
        transient, rest = eg.split(TransientError)
        print("retry?", transient is not None and rest is None)

On CPython 3.12 the failing call logged WARNING transient failures: ['web search timed out'] and ERROR terminal: wiki rejected query, then printed retry? False: a retry only makes sense when every member is transient. Log per class with except*, re-raise, and decide once with split. To answer from the sources that worked, use gather(..., return_exceptions=True) instead, because a TaskGroup cancels the other children on the first failure.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: An ExceptionGroup holds several exceptions, so a program can report failures that happened at the same time, the normal case in concurrent code. except* T handles the members matching T; unlike except, several clauses can run for one group, each seeing only its own part, and unmatched members are re-raised. TaskGroup raises a group whenever a child fails, which is why moving from gather to TaskGroup breaks except ValueError handlers.

Q · Mechanism — What does except* do with a group, step by step? Each clause effectively calls group.split(T): the leaves that are T instances, keeping the message and nesting, and the rest. The body runs with the matching subgroup bound to the variable, always a group. The rest moves on, so a group with a TransientError and a TerminalError runs both handlers. After the last clause, unmatched leaves are re-raised with tracebacks intact; a new exception raised in a clause is combined with them. That's why return is forbidden: the remaining clauses must still run.

⚖️ Compare

except T except* T
Handles one exception the T members of a group
Clauses that run the first match only every matching clause
Variable the exception itself always an ExceptionGroup
Unmatched parts n/a re-raised as a smaller group
return inside allowed SyntaxError

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A TaskGroup with one failing child raises that child's exception"
    ✅ It raises a group containing it; except ValueError doesn't match (see The idea).
  • ❌ "except* is except (A, B) with new syntax"
    ✅ except (A, B) runs one clause for one exception; except* splits a group and can run several.
  • 🔀 Not the same as chaining
    ↳ Difference: groups are horizontal, several independent failures at once; raise … from is vertical, one failure causing another. Each member can carry its own chain.
  • 🔀 Not the same as partial results
    ↳ Difference: a group reports failures only, and TaskGroup cancels siblings; for "whatever succeeded", use gather(return_exceptions=True).
  • ⚠️ Don't write except* ExceptionGroup.
    ↳ Why: it's a TypeError; catch the whole group with plain except ExceptionGroup.
  • 🔖 Version: ExceptionGroup, except* and TaskGroup are 3.11+ (PEP 654); the exceptiongroup backport gives the classes and catch(), not the syntax.
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.13.

🕸️ Connections

Path: exception model ─▶ exception groups ─▶ tasks & cancellation

  • Builds on the exception model: groups are ordinary exceptions on the same unwinding path.
  • Used by tasks & cancellation: TaskGroup is the main producer of groups.
  • Builds on custom exceptions: a transient-vs-terminal taxonomy is what except* branches on.
  • Used by reliability mechanics: retry only when split shows every member is transient.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Trio's MultiError was the prototype; JavaScript's AggregateError from Promise.any plays the same role.

notes.title: String Formatting & I/O
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Format specification mini-language · 📘 io: text vs binary streams, buffering · 📜 PEP 686: UTF-8 mode by default

⚡ TL;DR

f"{value:spec}" hands the spec to __format__: fill·align, sign, width, grouping, .precision, type. Text mode decodes with an encoding (always say utf-8); binary mode gives raw bytes; writes are buffered.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Format spec order? fill/align ─▶ sign ─▶ #/0 ─▶ width ─▶ ,/_ ─▶ .precision ─▶ type (d x b f e %).
What does f"{x=}" print? x= then the value: a debugging shortcut (3.8+).
Why always pass encoding=? Until 3.15 a bare open() uses the locale's encoding, which can be cp1252 on Windows.

💡 The idea

f-strings pass the spec to the object's __format__, so your own types can define a mini-language (Money below). The real hazard is I/O: a bare open(path) decodes with the locale's encoding, which varies by machine, until PEP 686 makes UTF-8 the default in 3.15. Text mode decodes and translates newlines; "rb" gives raw bytes (Unicode). Writes go through a buffer, io.DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE = 8192 bytes on 3.12 and 131072 on 3.14: output can look stuck until a flush.

💻 Code

import pathlib
class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents): self.cents = cents
    def __format__(self, spec): return f"${self.cents / 100:{spec or ',.2f'}}"
n, pi = 1234567, 3.14159
print(f"{n:,} {n:_x} {pi:8.2f}| {0.071:.1%} {pi=:.2f} {Money(123456)} {Money(5):.0f}")
p = pathlib.Path("demo.txt"); p.write_text("café\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(p.read_bytes(), len(p.read_bytes()), len(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
# → 1,234,567 12_d687     3.14| 7.1% pi=3.14 $1,234.56 $0
# → b'caf\xc3\xa9\n' 6 5      five characters, six bytes: é is two in UTF-8 (CPython 3.12)

notes.title: Text Processing & Unicode
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Unicode HOWTO · 📘 unicodedata · 📘 str.encode and error handlers

⚡ TL;DR

Decode once at the edge (named encoding, deliberate errors=), normalize before comparing, encode once on the way out. Bytes ≠ code points ≠ graphemes: len() counts code points, so cut byte budgets by encode-slice-decode.

🧭 Flow: bytes arrive ─▶ decode(encoding, errors=…) once, at the boundary ─▶ str of code points ─▶ NFC (or NFKC + casefold() for match keys) ─▶ clean, compare, slice ─▶ encode("utf-8") once on the way out

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Why is "café" == "café" false? Different code points (4 vs 5: é vs e + combining accent); NFC first.
lower() vs casefold()? casefold() is for matching: "Straße" → "strasse"; lower() keeps ß.
What does len("👨‍👩‍👧") return? 5 code points; one visible character; 18 UTF-8 bytes.

💡 The idea

Python 3's str is Unicode, so text seems solved, until three units disagree: characters as people see them, code points as Python counts them, and bytes as files carry them. On CPython 3.12:

"café" == "café"        # → False: both display as café
b"caf\xe9".decode("utf-8")         # → UnicodeDecodeError: … byte 0xe9 in position 3
"café".encode().decode("latin-1")  # → 'cafÃ©': wrong but valid, so no error at all
"👨‍👩‍👧"[:1]                          # → '👨': half a family

The last two are the dangerous ones: mojibake raises nothing, and slicing by code points cuts a character in half.

The trade: explicit decoding and normalization cost a little code at the edges, and in return the inside of the program never meets a surprise byte or an unequal "equal" string.

⚙️ How it works

The text boundary, with the decision at each step:

Rule What actually happens
Error handlers strict raises with byte offsets; replace writes U+FFFD (caf�), damage you can count; ignore hides loss; surrogateescape gives 'caf\udce9' and restores the exact bytes on encode, right for filenames.
Normalization NFC composes canonically equal forms. NFKC also folds compatibility forms, lossily: ﬁle → file, １２３ → 123, x² → x2, Ⅻ → XII.
Storage width PEP 393 stores a string at its widest character: 100 chars cost 141 bytes ASCII, 157 Latin-1, 258 €, 460 emoji.
translate fast path ASCII-only text and mapping: 1.9 µs on a 1,320-char sample; add two accented letters and 3.12 took 47.8 µs, slower than re.sub (~16 µs) and chained replace (~5 µs). 3.14 narrows it to 8.5 µs.
isdigit() is broad "²".isdigit() is True but int("²") raises ValueError; validate with isdecimal().

💻 Code

The text boundary of a document-ingestion pipeline:

import logging, re, unicodedata
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
_CONTROL = {c: None for c in range(32) if chr(c) not in "\t\n"} | {0x7F: None}
_SPACES = re.compile(r"\s+")

def decode_document(raw: bytes, source: str) -> str:
    """The one place bytes become text. Strict first, lossy only on purpose."""
    try:
        return raw.decode("utf-8-sig")                 # also strips a BOM
    except UnicodeDecodeError as exc:
        log.warning("%s: not UTF-8 at byte %d; replacing bad bytes", source, exc.start)
        return raw.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")   # U+FFFD marks the damage

def normalize_for_index(text: str) -> str:
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)         # ﬁ→fi, fullwidth→ASCII
    text = text.translate(_CONTROL)                    # drop control chars in one pass
    return _SPACES.sub(" ", text).strip()

def match_key(text: str) -> str:
    return normalize_for_index(text).casefold()        # compare and dedup, never display

def truncate_utf8(text: str, max_bytes: int) -> str:
    return text.encode("utf-8")[:max_bytes].decode("utf-8", errors="ignore")

On CPython 3.12, "﻿The ﬁle is\x00 at Straße １２\n" normalized to 'The file is at Straße 12' with key 'the file is at strasse 12'. A Latin-1 file logged legacy.csv: not UTF-8 at byte 3 and became 'caf� menu'. Both spellings of café gave one key, and truncate_utf8("naïve café", 11) returned 'naïve caf', where a plain slice-and-decode raised UnicodeDecodeError. Keys are for matching only: NFKC is lossy, so display keeps the original.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Decode bytes to str exactly once at the boundary, with an explicit encoding (utf-8-sig strips a BOM) and a deliberate error policy: fail for exact data, or replace and log the offset for bulk ingestion. Inside, normalize before comparing: NFC for equality, NFKC plus casefold() for search keys, keeping the original for display. len counts code points and storage limits are bytes, so truncate by encode-slice-decode, and encode once on the way out.

Q · Mechanism — A str.translate cleaner benchmarks well but is a hotspot on multilingual production text. Why, and what do you choose instead? translate has a fast path only when text and mapping are ASCII; one non-ASCII character drops it to a per-code-point dict lookup. On a 1,320-char sample, 3.12 went from 1.9 µs to 47.8 µs, 25× slower and slower than the regex. For a handful of fixed characters, chained replace stays around 5 µs either way; for classes or patterns, a precompiled re is predictable; translate suits big one-to-one maps over mostly ASCII. The lesson: benchmark string code on representative data, because speed and memory follow the widest character.

⚖️ Compare

Unit How to count "👨‍👩‍👧" Use for
Bytes (UTF-8) len(s.encode()) 18 storage limits, network, DB columns
Code points len(s) 5 Python indexing, most algorithms
Grapheme clusters len(regex.findall(r"\X", s)) 1 UI truncation, limits users see
Tokens tokenizer-specific varies LLM context budgets

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Python 3 strings are Unicode, so encoding problems are gone"
    ✅ They move to the boundary, and a wrong-but-valid decode produces mojibake with no error.
  • ❌ "len(s) is the characters the user sees"
    ✅ It's code points: regex's \X found 8 graphemes in the 13 code points of "café 👨‍👩‍👧 🇮🇳".
  • 🔀 Not the same as cleaning text for a model
    ↳ Difference: normalization makes equal text compare equal; stripping boilerplate or lowercasing for a model are task choices made on a copy.
  • ⚠️ Don't store NFKC or casefolded text as the canonical copy.
    ↳ Why: both are lossy (x² → x2); use them for keys.
  • ⚠️ Don't use errors="ignore" on ingestion.
    ↳ Why: it hides data loss; replace and log, or fail.
  • ⚠️ Don't trust a string benchmark run on ASCII.
    ↳ Why: translate speed and memory change with the widest character.
  • 🔖 Version: flexible string storage 3.3+ (PEP 393); UTF-8 default text encoding 3.15 (PEP 686), so pass encoding= until then.
    ↳ Note: timings on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6, indicative only.

🕸️ Connections

  • Builds on str internals: why memory and translate speed follow the widest character.
  • Used by the validation boundary: normalize text fields at the same edge where input is validated.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java and JavaScript strings are UTF-16 code units, so their length miscounts emoji too.
